PixelFlow: third-party notices

================================================================================

This file opens with PixelFlow's own notice: its licence, and its credit to
xLights and to the other work that parts of it are derived from. After that
comes the third-party software and data PixelFlow includes. Each is the work of
its own authors and is provided under its own licence. This file lists them
(part 1) and reproduces their licence texts (parts 2 and 3).

This file is generated from the app's lockfiles by scripts/licenses.mjs. Do not
edit it by hand.

Credit: xLights
===============

PixelFlow is an independent project. It was inspired by xLights, the sequencer
the holiday lighting community has built and relied on for many years, and it
can import xLights shows and sequences. It is not xLights and is not affiliated
with or endorsed by the xLights project. Its design, its engine, and most of
its code are its own.

Some parts of PixelFlow are derived from xLights' source code, and are not only
inspired by it. They are: a number of the renderer's effects; rules every layer
passes through, such as blending, blur, and line drawing; the model geometry
that puts each pixel of a prop where xLights puts it, for imported props and
for several of PixelFlow's own shapes; value curves; and tables of defaults,
ranges, and shapes. Those parts are used under xLights'
licence, the GNU General Public License, version 3, and that is why PixelFlow
as a whole is offered under the same licence.

    xLights
    https://github.com/xLightsSequencer/xLights
    Copyright (C) the xLights authors and contributors
    Licensed under the GNU General Public License, version 3

The file-by-file record of what is derived, with the xLights file each one
follows, is docs/licensing/provenance.md in PixelFlow's source. Each of those
files also names the xLights file it follows in its opening comment.

Thank you to everyone who has written and maintained xLights. PixelFlow could
not have been made without their work.

The list gets shorter over time. Where PixelFlow can do a part better with a
design of its own, that part is rewritten from a description of what it shows
and moves out of the derived list: Pinwheel, Shockwave and Plasma so far. The
rest stays, credited here.


Other borrowed work
===================

The mouth-shape table (which mouth a sound is sung with) is the one xLights
uses, which came to xLights from Papagayo:

    Papagayo
    Copyright (C) 2005 Mike Clifton
    Licensed under the GNU General Public License, version 2 or any later
    version; used in PixelFlow under version 3

Two ways of resizing a picture follow wxWidgets, so that a picture imported
from an xLights sequence is sized as it was there:

    wxWidgets
    https://github.com/wxWidgets/wxWidgets
    Copyright (C) the wxWidgets authors
    Licensed under the wxWindows Library Licence, version 3.1

The packages PixelFlow is built from, and the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary that
is built into it, are listed with their licences in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt,
which comes with the app.

END OF ACADEMIC FREE LICENSE. The following is intended to describe the essential
differences between the Academic Free License (AFL) version 1.0 and other
open source licenses:

The Academic Free License is similar to the BSD, MIT, UoI/NCSA and Apache
licenses in many respects but it is intended to solve a few problems with
those licenses.

* The AFL is written so as to make it clear what software is being
licensed (by the inclusion of a statement following the copyright notice
in the software). This way, the license functions better than a template
license. The BSD, MIT and UoI/NCSA licenses apply to unidentified software.

* The AFL contains a complete copyright grant to the software. The BSD
and Apache licenses are vague and incomplete in that respect.

* The AFL contains a complete patent grant to the software. The BSD, MIT,
UoI/NCSA and Apache licenses rely on an implied patent license and contain
no explicit patent grant.

* The AFL makes it clear that no trademark rights are granted to the
licensor's trademarks. The Apache license contains such a provision, but the
BSD, MIT and UoI/NCSA licenses do not.

* The AFL includes the warranty by the licensor that it either owns the
copyright or that it is distributing the software under a license. None of
the other licenses contain that warranty. All other warranties are disclaimed,
as is the case for the other licenses.

* The AFL is itself copyrighted (with the right granted to copy and distribute
without modification). This ensures that the owner of the copyright to the
license will control changes. The Apache license contains a copyright notice,
but the BSD, MIT and UoI/NCSA licenses do not.
